fields.name: demonstration
fields.description: At the video cycle, write all supplied V frame labels in chronological order, including the last frame. At every act cycle copy the incoming list unchanged; do not replace demonstration images with execution images. If no demonstration has yet been supplied, write an empty list. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V112", "V128", "V144", "V160", "V176", "V192", "V208", "V222"]
fields.annotation: The ordered list of every frame label supplied in the video cycle, including the last frame. This preserves the demonstrated manipulation: which peg was selected, where along that peg it was grasped, and the approach and insertion geometry. Write the list at the video cycle and carry it unchanged through every act cycle. Before a video has been supplied the value is an empty list. e.g. ["V0", "V16", "V32", "V48", "V64", "V80", "V96", "V112", "V128", "V144", "V160", "V176", "V192", "V208", "V222"]

action:
At a video cycle output memory only. Execution starts with the open hand above the scene. Read demonstration to identify the peg actually lifted, the particular colored end between the fingers, and the box face entered by the other end. Track the selected peg backward to its initial position; do not select by color alone, since multiple pegs can share colors. Distinguish grasping an end from inserting that end: the free end enters the box. The selected box face can be on either image side. Robot left is +y, which appears on the right of the front image.

Use calibrated image geometry rather than copying episode-specific world coordinates. Recover tabletop peg axes and endpoints by intersecting camera rays with their appropriate height planes. With world-to-camera extrinsics [R|t], use camera center C = -R^T t and world ray direction d = R^T K^-1[u,v,1]^T. For a landmark at height h, compute lambda = (h - C_z)/d_z and X = C + lambda d before measuring world distances. Use the landmark's height, not automatically the tabletop height. Distinguish visible top-surface landmarks, the peg centerline, inner finger surfaces, and the TCP between the fingertips. Intersect a visible surface pixel at that surface's height, not at centerline height; recover the centerline and opposing-contact midpoint using the fitted peg cross-section and finger geometry. A visible finger edge is not the contact midpoint. When contact is hidden, constrain it with both opposing fingers and the rigid peg across neighboring demonstration frames rather than substituting an exposed colored point. Retain numerical precision through fitting and waypoint output; do not round coordinates to centimetres. Fit the box footprint and orientation from its edges. Use the wrist image to refine visible geometry. Use its supplied camera extrinsics and the reported TCP pose to recover visible held-peg landmarks in hand-relative coordinates; do not assume the wrist-image center is the TCP. At open-hand approach, use the wrist view to refine current peg landmarks without redefining the demonstrated contact as the reached TCP. Determine peg identity, grasped end, and contact position separately. Fit the whole peg and the opposing fingertip contacts together across closing and early lifting demonstration frames. Track both colored segments, their boundary, and the contact region back to the unobstructed initial peg. The grasped segment is the one enclosed by the fingers; neither prominence nor visibility in the wrist image establishes whether a segment is held or free. Track both ends through lift and transport and check which remains free during insertion to confirm the grasped end. Define a directed unit peg axis a from the held end toward the free end and locate the color boundary b. Fit the midpoint c of opposing fingertip contacts jointly with the peg endpoints and boundary; recover its signed longitudinal offset s = (c - b) dot a, rather than assuming contact at a segment center. Fit the directed axis from full peg edges and endpoints in calibrated world geometry, not from the front-image line angle. Check the contact's distance from both the boundary and the held endpoint, and require the same longitudinal contact to explain the opposing fingers across closure and early lift. Before choosing the approach or closing descent, reconstruct the current boundary and axis at peg height and map the demonstrated contact to b_current + s a_current in the tabletop plane. Refit these landmarks in the elevated open-hand view even when the resulting descent corrects more than a centimetre of approach tracking error. Do not substitute the peg midpoint, segment midpoint, or reached TCP for this contact. At pickup use a downward hand, roll approximately -pi and pitch approximately zero, align the hand's longitudinal axis with the peg, and close across its width; choose the yaw equivalent that matches the demonstration. For later manipulation, reconstruct the demonstrated orientation rather than imposing zero pitch.

Apply the following rules according to the observed pose, held object, and motion frames, not according to cycle number. If the hand is empty and not yet above the demonstrated grasp location, move open to that location at z=0.20 m with the pickup yaw. If it is open above that location near z=0.20 m, descend to the same nominal x,y at z=0.01 m and close. Recompute the nominal contact location from the visible peg geometry at the elevated open-hand configuration, not from the reached TCP. Use this same nominal x,y for the open approach, closing descent, and pickup lift. A reached approach displaced by more than a centimetre does not imply that the intended approach and contact locations differ. If the fingers have closed around the selected peg near table height, lift closed to z=0.20 m at that same nominal location and yaw.

If the selected peg has been lifted but has not yet been transported to the insertion approach, move closed to the demonstrated elevated transport endpoint. Separate endpoint selection from pose fitting. First identify the transition from completed lateral relocation and rotation to descent, then independently identify the transition from descent to inward movement for low staging. Fit each transition's contact pose using adjacent frames; an earlier sample during relocation is not the completed transport endpoint. Use one ordered landmark correspondence—held endpoint, color boundary, free endpoint, and opposing fingertip-contact midpoint—from closure and early lift through pickup, transport, staging, and rigid insertion. Verify that the free endpoint leads into the opening. Fit the contact within the held segment rather than snapping it to the boundary. Enforce the resulting shared peg-to-hand transform across these fits; do not independently refit the grasp offset to make an incorrect target appear consistent. Evaluate longitudinal and transverse landmark residuals separately: matching height or projected axis angle alone does not validate TCP translation. Visible relative hand/peg movement marks a change in this rigid relationship and must be distinguished from the preceding rigid insertion. Fit transport height and orientation independently of pickup; do not inherit pickup's z=0.20 m or exactly downward orientation. Fit each pose relative to the entered box face using neighboring demonstration frames, visible peg edges and endpoints, color boundary, and the midpoint between opposing fingertip contacts. Recover the rigid peg-to-TCP offset and constrain the actual held-peg offset with the current wrist image. Fit candidate hand rotation R_hand and TCP translation jointly by reprojecting the rigid peg and contact landmarks into the calibrated demonstration views: each landmark has world position p_TCP + R_hand r, where r is its fitted hand-relative offset. Compare projected endpoints, color boundary, peg edges, and opposing finger contacts with the observed geometry, using neighboring frames to resolve occlusion and the end of motion. Enforce p_TCP = p_landmark - R_hand r consistently across visible landmarks. Constrain rotation with both the directed held-to-free axis and finger-contact arrangement, not an unsigned image line angle. Accept transport and staging estimates only after checking their landmark reprojections; neither arbitrary face clearance nor the image boundary locates a clipped TCP. Use these same contact constraints to reconstruct low staging independently, without rounding coordinates or lowering from the measured transport endpoint. If the hand is partly outside the image, infer its position from the visible held peg and demonstrated grasp offset, not an arbitrary clearance beyond the face. Project elevated geometry at its elevated height, not onto the tabletop. The TCP is neither the free tip nor the opening center. Resolve yaw's pi ambiguity by transforming the ordered peg landmarks under each candidate hand rotation using the shared peg-to-hand transform. Reject candidates that reverse the established held/free correspondence or fail to explain the opposing contacts together with the endpoints and boundary. Do not refit the grasp offset to rescue a reversed candidate, and do not assume that the positive hand axis points toward the free tip. Preserve demonstrated non-cardinal orientations. Reproduce demonstrated transport tilt and height; approximately 0.19 m is only an initial estimate for nearly level transport, not a universal target. Do not assume the transport endpoint lies directly above low staging, and do not move directly from pickup into the opening.

If the hand is at the elevated transport endpoint, move closed to the independently reconstructed low staging pose immediately before inward entry. Compute its intended box-relative position rather than preserving the measured transport endpoint. Ordinary transport tracking error is not evidence of a demonstrated inward translation during descent; include such translation only when the demonstrated geometry supports it. Reconstruct height and pitch together so the free tip approaches the opening correctly. For nearly level staging, TCP height near 0.04 m is an initial estimate, not an invariant; preserve demonstrated lower or tilted staging when present. If the hand is at completed low staging, target the endpoint of the demonstrated first inward alignment advance, not an arbitrary sampled image along that advance. For the nearly level entry pattern, this advance is approximately 0.05 m along the inward face normal, with demonstrated lateral and height corrections. Compute it from the reconstructed nominal staging pose rather than simply adding displacement to the reached TCP. Entry may instead combine inward translation with substantial height and pitch correction when supported by the demonstration. Align the free tip with the opening, not the TCP, and keep the gripper closed.

After an inward advance, compare the current motion frames and peg-to-opening relationship with the demonstrated motion segments. Video frames sample motion; they are not a list of commanded waypoints. Identify completed staging, the endpoint of the first inward alignment advance, and terminal insertion from neighboring frames and changes in translation, height, or orientation. Require evidence of a distinct completed intermediate maneuver before selecting another intermediate target; an intervening sampled pose or a still-exposed free tip alone is not such evidence. Once the first alignment advance has completed, target terminal insertion unless a distinct further alignment maneuver is supported. Preserve any such demonstrated maneuver, including tilted-entry corrections, rather than skipping it. Reconstruct target geometry without a universal advance length or 0.05 m cap. Through an otherwise straight insertion advance, preserve the established insertion-axis orientation; change it only when peg-axis and fingertip-contact geometry support the change, not merely because the projected arm or wrist silhouette changes. When terminal insertion is the next appropriate configuration, first identify the end of the demonstrated inward maneuver that preserves the established rigid, closed-grasp peg-to-hand relationship. Track the ordered peg landmarks and opposing contacts through the remaining demonstration, using neighboring frames to distinguish relative hand/peg movement from occlusion or projection changes. If subsequent hand motion changes that relationship, select the end of rigid insertion before that change; do not deepen the target using the later hand position or fit a new grasp offset to explain it. If the relationship remains unchanged through the end, use the final demonstration configuration. A success indicator corroborates insertion but does not identify a subsequent waypoint or release command. Reconstruct the entered face plane and opposing fingertip-contact midpoint at this selected rigid-insertion endpoint. A short remaining advance is permissible; impose no minimum insertion distance. If the sampled views do not establish the endpoint, do not invent an exact command boundary. Express that contact relative to the face as separate inward-normal distance, lateral alignment, and height. Map this face-relative geometry to the current box and recover the TCP using the fitted grasp offset. Check the inferred TCP standoff against the remaining exposed peg length and contact geometry. Map the proposed terminal target back into the demonstration's box-relative frame and reproject its hand and peg landmarks, using the shared grasp transform, into the views supporting the selected rigid-insertion endpoint. Compare the predicted opposing fingertip-contact landmarks with the fingers at that endpoint, and the predicted exposed peg between contact and entered face with its visible exposed length. Reject a depth fit that places contact farther inward than those endpoint fingers, even if its free tip would lie securely inside the box. Do not use fingers from subsequent relative hand/peg motion for this stopping check. Check inward-normal distance, lateral alignment, and height separately; free-tip alignment alone does not validate terminal depth. Do not advance until the TCP approaches the face, place it at the opening, infer depth from the free tip alone, or impose a fixed remaining travel distance. This terminal-depth fit applies only when terminal insertion is the next supported target; it does not establish an otherwise unobserved intermediate stopping point. Keep the gripper closed through the demonstrated pickup lift, transport, staging, and insertion motions. A red indicator confirms successful insertion but specifies neither an additional waypoint nor a gripper command. Apply any separately supplied post-success action convention; do not extrapolate an unseen continuation from the terminal demonstration image.

Use the current motion frames to distinguish a completed lift from completed transport and a completed descent from completed horizontal insertion. Compare the current configuration to the retained demonstration when the current wrist view shows only the held peg or table; do not interpret an occluded box as a missing box. Allow approximately centimetre-scale tracking error when recognizing a completed long move, but compute the next waypoint from the intended geometry.

For an unlisted or uncertain configuration, localize the held peg, box, and closest demonstrated configuration again. If holding the peg with uncertain clearance, lift vertically to safe clearance before correcting alignment; if empty, approach the demonstrated peg open. Never insert blindly when the free tip is visibly misaligned. Use a small corrective waypoint when necessary, and never issue an identical TCP waypoint merely to change the gripper. No purposeless waiting is required.
